name: Trihexyphenidyl Hydrochloride
sections: White crystalline powder (hydrochloride), slightly soluble in water.
One of the oldest synthetic antiparkinsonian agents; remains widely used for drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms and dystonia. First approval/introduction: US FDA 1949 (Parkinson's disease).

Blocks central muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the striatum, restoring the dopamine–acetylcholine balance disturbed by dopamine-receptor blockade or dopamine loss. Reduces drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms, tremor and rigidity. Receptor / target profile: Antagonist at all five muscarinic receptors with much stronger activity at M1 and M4.
Summary: Rapidly absorbed; onset within 1 h, peak 2–3 h, duration 6–12 h. Excreted mainly in urine.
Drug-induced extrapyramidal disorders (antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism, acute dystonia)
Parkinsonism – adjunct to levodopa or monotherapy in younger patients
Drug-induced EPS: 1 mg initially, increase gradually to 5–15 mg/day in 3–4 divided doses
Usual maintenance: 2 mg two to three times daily
Parkinsonism: 1 mg day 1, increase by 2 mg every 3–5 days to 6–10 mg/day in divided doses
Elderly: start low, use lowest effective dose
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Highly susceptible to confusion, memory impairment, urinary retention and constipation – avoid if possible (Beers criteria).
Used in dystonia/cerebral palsy at specialist level; safety in young children not established.
Safety not established; use only if clearly needed.
May suppress lactation; use with caution.
Obstructive disease of GI or genitourinary tract (e.g. prostatic hypertrophy with retention, paralytic ileus)
Heat intolerance due to reduced sweating
Other anticholinergics (TCAs, antihistamines, phenothiazines) – additive effects
May reduce absorption of drugs due to slowed gastric emptying
Take with meals; avoid alcohol; ensure fluid intake in hot weather.
Intraocular pressure periodically on long-term use; cognition in elderly; bowel and bladder function.
Anticholinergic toxicity: hot dry skin, mydriasis, tachycardia, hyperthermia, delirium, hallucinations. Supportive care; physostigmine may be considered under specialist supervision.
Burke et al., Neurology 1986 – high-dose trihexyphenidyl effective in idiopathic torsion dystonia (double-blind crossover).
WHO mhGAP guidance: anticholinergics should not be used routinely for prophylaxis of EPS but for treatment of established symptoms.
May cause dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation
Avoid hot environments and strenuous exercise in heat
Do not take more than prescribed (risk of misuse)
Report confusion or difficulty passing urine
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
